name: Zorah
what: A town in the Shephelah west of Jerusalem, the hometown of Samson's family.
today: Tel Tzora, near Beit Shemesh in Israel.
key: Zorah was allotted to Dan (Joshua 19).
The angel of the Lord announced Samson's birth to Manoah's wife of Zorah (Judges 13).
Samson was buried between Zorah and Eshtaol in his father's tomb (Judges 16).
The Danites sent spies from Zorah to find new land (Judges 18).
Rehoboam fortified Zorah (2 Chronicles 11).

name: Pisgah
what: A mountain peak or ridge in the Abarim range overlooking the Jordan Valley.
today: Near Mount Nebo in Jordan; possibly Ras es-Siyagha.
key: Israel journeyed to the top of Pisgah overlooking the desert (Numbers 21).
Balak took Balaam to the top of Pisgah to curse Israel (Numbers 23).
God told Moses to view the land from Pisgah but not to cross (Deuteronomy 3).
Moses went up to the top of Pisgah, where God showed him the land (Deuteronomy 34).

name: Peor
what: A mountain in Moab where Balaam was taken and where Israel later worshiped Baal of Peor.
today: In Moab near Mount Nebo, Jordan; exact site unknown.
key: Balak takes Balaam to the top of Peor to curse Israel (Numbers 23).
Israel yokes itself to Baal of Peor, and a plague follows (Numbers 25).
Moses says Balaam's advice caused Israel to sin at Peor (Numbers 31).
Phinehas recalls the sin at Peor when confronting the eastern tribes (Joshua 22).

name: Baal-peor
what: A site in Moab where Israel worshiped the local god Baal and fell into sexual immorality.
today: Exact site unknown; in the plains of Moab near Mount Nebo, Jordan.
key: Moses reminds Israel that the LORD destroyed everyone who followed the Baal of Peor (Deuteronomy 4).
The psalmist recalls how Israel joined the Baal of Peor and provoked God's anger (Psalms 106).
Hosea points back to Baal-peor as the place Israel first devoted itself to shameful idolatry (Hosea 9).

name: En-rogel
what: A spring just outside Jerusalem where the Kidron and Hinnom valleys meet.
today: Likely Bir Ayyub, just south of the City of David, Jerusalem.
key: En-rogel marks part of Judah's northern boundary (Joshua 15).
En-rogel marks part of Benjamin's southern boundary (Joshua 18).
Jonathan and Ahimaaz wait at En-rogel to carry news to David during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 17).
Adonijah sacrifices near En-rogel while trying to make himself king (1 Kings 1).

name: Topheth
what: A site in the Valley of Hinnom where children were burned as offerings.
today: In the Hinnom Valley south of Jerusalem's Old City; exact spot unknown.
key: Josiah defiled Topheth so no one could sacrifice children there to Molech (2 Kings 23).
Jeremiah condemned Topheth and said it would be called the Valley of Slaughter (Jeremiah 7).
Jeremiah broke a clay flask, warning that God would make Jerusalem like Topheth (Jeremiah 19).

name: Valley of the Son of Hinnom
what: A valley south of Jerusalem where idolatrous child sacrifice was practiced.
today: The valley along the west and south sides of Jerusalem's Old City.
key: Josiah defiled Topheth in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom (2 Kings 23).
King Ahaz burned his sons as offerings in this valley (2 Chronicles 28).
King Manasseh also burned his sons as offerings there (2 Chronicles 33).
Jeremiah said the valley would be renamed the Valley of Slaughter (Jeremiah 7).
Judah built high places of Baal in the valley to offer children to Molech (Jeremiah 32).

name: Washer's Field
what: A field outside Jerusalem's walls by the conduit of the upper pool, where cloth was washed.
today: Exact site unknown; just outside ancient Jerusalem's walls.
key: Assyria's officials stood by the Washer's Field to demand Jerusalem's surrender (2 Kings 18).
Isaiah met King Ahaz by the conduit on the highway to the Washer's Field (Isaiah 7).
Isaiah records the Rabshakeh's arrival at the same spot during Hezekiah's reign (Isaiah 36).

name: Valley of Hinnom
what: A valley along the south and west sides of Jerusalem, later notorious for idolatrous child sacrifice.
today: Ge Hinnom, below the south and west walls of Jerusalem's Old City.
key: Judah's northern boundary ran through the Valley of Hinnom, south of the Jebusite city (Joshua 15).
Benjamin's southern boundary went down the Valley of Hinnom (Joshua 18).
After the exile, people of Judah settled from Beersheba as far as the Valley of Hinnom (Nehemiah 11).

name: Valley of Slaughter
what: Jeremiah's name of judgment for the Valley of Hinnom, where children were sacrificed.
today: The Hinnom Valley, south of Jerusalem's Old City.
key: Jeremiah condemned Topheth and said it would be called the Valley of Slaughter (Jeremiah 7).
Jeremiah broke a clay flask in the valley, repeating that it would be called the Valley of Slaughter (Jeremiah 19).

name: Kiriath-jearim
what: A Gibeonite town west of Jerusalem where the ark of the covenant stayed for twenty years.
today: Likely Tel Kiriath-jearim, near Abu Ghosh, west of Jerusalem
key: Kiriath-jearim was one of the Gibeonite cities that made peace with Israel (Joshua 9).
The ark was brought to the house of Abinadab in Kiriath-jearim (1 Samuel 7).
David brought the ark up from Kiriath-jearim (1 Chronicles 13).
The prophet Uriah of Kiriath-jearim was executed by King Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 26).

name: Baalah
what: Another name for Kiriath-jearim, a town on Judah's northern border where the ark rested for years.
today: Kiriath-jearim, likely at Deir el-Azar near Abu Ghosh, west of Jerusalem.
key: Baalah, identified as Kiriath-jearim, marks part of Judah's northern boundary (Joshua 15).
David and all Israel went to Baalah to bring the ark of God up from there (1 Chronicles 13).

name: Bethany
what: A village on the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem, home of Mary, Martha, and Lazarus.
today: Al-Eizariya, about 3 km east of Jerusalem in the West Bank.
key: Jesus stayed overnight in Bethany during his final week (Matthew 21).
A woman anointed Jesus at the home of Simon the leper in Bethany (Mark 14).
Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead in Bethany (John 11).
Mary anointed Jesus' feet at a dinner in Bethany six days before Passover (John 12).
Jesus led his disciples out as far as Bethany and was carried up into heaven (Luke 24).

name: Kidron
what: The valley and seasonal stream between Jerusalem's temple hill and the Mount of Olives.
today: The Kidron Valley, east of Jerusalem's Old City.
key: David crossed the brook Kidron as he fled from Absalom (2 Samuel 15).
Solomon warned Shimei that crossing the Kidron would cost his life (1 Kings 2).
Asa burned his grandmother's Asherah image at the brook Kidron (1 Kings 15).
Josiah burned the idolatrous objects from the temple in the Kidron Valley (2 Kings 23).
Hezekiah's Levites carried the temple's uncleanness out to the Kidron (2 Chronicles 29).

name: Valley of Jehoshaphat
what: The valley where Joel foresees God gathering the nations for judgment.
today: Exact site unknown; traditionally the Kidron Valley east of Jerusalem.
key: God will gather all nations there and judge them for scattering his people Israel (Joel 3).
The nations are summoned to the valley, where God will sit to judge them (Joel 3).
Multitudes fill the valley of decision as the day of the Lord draws near (Joel 3).

name: Gihon
what: The main spring of ancient Jerusalem, in the Kidron Valley below the City of David.
today: The Gihon Spring in the City of David, Jerusalem.
key: Solomon was anointed king at Gihon (1 Kings 1).
Hezekiah closed the upper outlet of Gihon and channeled water into the city (2 Chronicles 32).
Manasseh built an outer wall west of Gihon (2 Chronicles 33).

name: Dan
what: The original tribal territory of Dan, west of Benjamin toward the Mediterranean coast.
today: The area between Jerusalem and Tel Aviv in central Israel.
key: Dan received the seventh lot, including Zorah, Eshtaol, and Joppa's vicinity (Joshua 19).
The Amorites pressed the Danites back into the hill country (Judges 1).
Lacking an inheritance, the Danites migrated north and seized Laish, renaming it Dan (Judges 18).

name: Judah
what: The southern kingdom ruled by David's descendants from Jerusalem after Israel divided.
today: Southern Israel and the southern West Bank, centered on Jerusalem.
key: After the kingdom divided, Rehoboam reigned over the people of Judah (1 Kings 12).
A man of God from Judah denounced Jeroboam's altar at Bethel (1 Kings 13).
Rehoboam built fortified cities for defense in Judah (2 Chronicles 11).
Syria and Israel threatened Judah, and Isaiah urged Ahaz to trust God (Isaiah 7).
Sennacherib of Assyria attacked all the fortified cities of Judah in Hezekiah's reign (2 Kings 18).

name: Beth-jeshimoth
what: A town on the plains of Moab near the Jordan, at the edge of Israel's last wilderness camp.
today: Likely Tell el-Azeimeh, northeast of the Dead Sea, Jordan.
key: Israel camps along the Jordan from Beth-jeshimoth to Abel-shittim (Numbers 33).
Beth-jeshimoth marks a boundary of the kingdom of Sihon (Joshua 12).
Beth-jeshimoth is allotted to the tribe of Reuben (Joshua 13).
Ezekiel names Beth-jeshimoth among Moab's glorious cities facing judgment (Ezekiel 25).

name: Jerusalem
what: The city David made Israel's capital, site of God's temple and of Jesus' death and resurrection.
today: Jerusalem, Israel
key: David captured the Jebusite stronghold and made Jerusalem his royal city (2 Samuel 5).
Solomon dedicated the temple, and the glory of the LORD filled it (1 Kings 8).
The Babylonians burned the temple and the city and carried the people into exile (2 Kings 25).
Jesus was crucified just outside the city and laid in a nearby tomb (Luke 23).
The Holy Spirit came upon the disciples at Pentecost, and about three thousand believed (Acts 2).

name: Zion
what: The hill in Jerusalem David captured; the name extends to the temple mount, the city, and God's people.
today: Jerusalem, Israel
key: David captured the stronghold of Zion and called it the city of David (2 Samuel 5).
Solomon brought the ark up from Zion into the new temple (1 Kings 8).
God declares that he has set his King on Zion, his holy hill (Psalms 2).
Isaiah foresaw the law going out from Zion to the nations (Isaiah 2).
Peter applies Isaiah's cornerstone laid in Zion to Christ (1 Peter 2).

name: Judea
what: The southern region around Jerusalem, the former territory of Judah, a Roman district in New Testament times.
today: Southern Israel and the West Bank around Jerusalem
key: Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea (Matthew 2).
John the Baptist preached in the wilderness of Judea (Matthew 3).
Jesus returned to Judea to raise Lazarus (John 11).
Jesus sent his disciples to be witnesses in Judea, Samaria, and beyond (Acts 1).
Men from Judea taught that Gentiles must be circumcised, prompting the Jerusalem council (Acts 15).

name: Mount Zion
what: The hill of Jerusalem where God dwelt in his temple, also a picture of the heavenly city.
today: Jerusalem, Israel
key: God promised Hezekiah that a remnant would go out from Mount Zion (2 Kings 19).
Mount Zion is praised as the city of the great King (Psalms 48).
Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved (Psalms 125).
Believers have come to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12).
John saw the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with the 144,000 (Revelation 14).

name: Beyond the River
what: The Persian province west of the Euphrates River, which included Judah.
today: Modern Syria, Lebanon, Israel, the Palestinian territories, and Jordan
key: Officials of the province Beyond the River wrote to Artaxerxes against Jerusalem (Ezra 4).
Tattenai, governor of the province Beyond the River, questioned the temple rebuilding (Ezra 5).
Darius ordered the province's treasury to pay for the temple work (Ezra 6).
Nehemiah carried the king's letters to the governors of the province Beyond the River (Nehemiah 2).

name: Holy Place
what: The outer sacred room of the tabernacle and temple, in front of the Most Holy Place.
today: Solomon's temple stood on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem; it no longer exists.
key: When the priests came out of the Holy Place, the cloud of the Lord's glory filled the temple (1 Kings 8).
Hezekiah ordered the Levites to carry the filth out of the Holy Place and restore worship (2 Chronicles 29).
Ezekiel's guide measured the nave of the visionary temple (Ezekiel 41).
Hebrews describes the tabernacle's first section, with the lampstand and table, as the Holy Place (Hebrews 9).

name: Most Holy Place
what: The innermost room of the tabernacle and temple, where the ark of the covenant was kept.
today: Solomon's temple stood on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem; it no longer exists.
key: Solomon built the inner sanctuary, overlaid it with gold, and placed two olivewood cherubim inside (1 Kings 6).
The priests brought the ark into the Most Holy Place beneath the cherubim's wings (1 Kings 8).
Aaron and his sons served the Most Holy Place and made atonement for Israel (1 Chronicles 6).
Ezekiel's guide measured the Most Holy Place of the visionary temple (Ezekiel 41).

name: Millo
what: A terraced earthwork or fortification in Jerusalem's City of David, built up by David and Solomon.
today: Likely the stepped stone structure in the City of David, Jerusalem.
key: David built up the city around the Millo after capturing Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5).
Solomon used forced labor to build the Millo (1 Kings 9).
Jeroboam rebelled against Solomon while the Millo was being built (1 Kings 11).
Hezekiah strengthened the Millo before Assyria's attack (2 Chronicles 32).

name: Corner Gate
what: A gate at the northwest corner of Jerusalem's city wall.
today: Exact site unknown; likely at the northwest corner of ancient Jerusalem.
key: Jehoash of Israel broke down Jerusalem's wall to the Corner Gate (2 Kings 14).
Uzziah built towers at the Corner Gate (2 Chronicles 26).
Jeremiah foretold the city's rebuilding to the Corner Gate (Jeremiah 31).
Zechariah described Jerusalem secure from the Corner Gate onward (Zechariah 14).

name: Jebus
what: The Jebusite city that David captured and made Jerusalem, his capital.
today: The City of David, in Jerusalem.
key: Jebus, that is Jerusalem, was listed among Benjamin's cities (Joshua 18).
A Levite refused to stay overnight in Jebus because it was foreign (Judges 19).
David captured Jebus and the stronghold of Zion (1 Chronicles 11).

name: House of the Forest of Lebanon
what: A great hall in Solomon's palace complex in Jerusalem, built with rows of cedar pillars.
today: Not preserved; it stood in Solomon's palace complex in Jerusalem.
key: Solomon built the House of the Forest of Lebanon with cedar pillars and beams (1 Kings 7).
Solomon placed hundreds of gold shields there and used gold drinking vessels (1 Kings 10).
Chronicles records the same gold shields in the house (2 Chronicles 9).

name: Ophel
what: The fortified hill between the City of David and the temple in Jerusalem.
today: The ridge just south of the Temple Mount in Jerusalem.
key: Jotham built extensively on the wall of Ophel (2 Chronicles 27).
Manasseh carried Jerusalem's outer wall around Ophel (2 Chronicles 33).
Temple servants living on Ophel helped repair the wall (Nehemiah 3).
The temple servants lived on Ophel after the exile (Nehemiah 11).

name: Dung Gate
what: A gate in the southern wall of ancient Jerusalem, rebuilt in Nehemiah's day.
today: Southern end of ancient Jerusalem; not the Old City's modern Dung Gate.
key: Nehemiah inspects the broken walls by night, passing the Dung Gate (Nehemiah 2).
Malchijah son of Rechab repairs the Dung Gate (Nehemiah 3).
One thanksgiving choir marches on the wall toward the Dung Gate at its dedication (Nehemiah 12).

name: Benjamin Gate
what: A gate on the north side of Jerusalem facing the territory of Benjamin.
today: North side of ancient Jerusalem; exact site unknown.
key: Pashhur beats Jeremiah and puts him in the stocks in the upper Benjamin Gate (Jeremiah 20).
Jeremiah is arrested at the Benjamin Gate and accused of deserting to the Chaldeans (Jeremiah 37).
Ebed-melech appeals for Jeremiah while King Zedekiah sits in the Benjamin Gate (Jeremiah 38).
Zechariah foresees Jerusalem restored from the Benjamin Gate to the Corner Gate (Zechariah 14).

name: Salem
what: The city of Melchizedek, king and priest, generally identified with Jerusalem.
today: Generally identified with Jerusalem.
key: Melchizedek king of Salem brings out bread and wine and blesses Abram (Genesis 14).
The psalmist says God's abode has been established in Salem (Psalms 76).
Hebrews explains that king of Salem means king of peace (Hebrews 7).

name: Sheep Gate
what: A gate in the northern wall of Jerusalem near the temple, beside the pool of Bethesda.
today: Northeast of the temple area in Jerusalem's Old City; exact site unknown.
key: Eliashib and the priests rebuild and consecrate the Sheep Gate (Nehemiah 3).
The thanksgiving procession passes the Sheep Gate at the wall's dedication (Nehemiah 12).
Jesus heals a man by the pool near the Sheep Gate (John 5).

name: Tower of Hananel
what: A tower on the northern wall of Jerusalem, near the Sheep Gate.
today: North wall of ancient Jerusalem; exact site unknown.
key: The priests rebuild the wall as far as the Tower of Hananel (Nehemiah 3).
The thanksgiving procession passes the Tower of Hananel (Nehemiah 12).
God promises the city will be rebuilt from the Tower of Hananel to the Corner Gate (Jeremiah 31).
Zechariah foresees Jerusalem inhabited from the Tower of Hananel to the king's winepresses (Zechariah 14).

name: Water Gate
what: A gate on the east side of Jerusalem where Ezra read the Law to the people.
today: East side of the City of David, near the Gihon Spring; exact site unknown.
key: Temple servants living on the Ophel repair up to a point opposite the Water Gate (Nehemiah 3).
Ezra reads the Book of the Law to the people in the square before the Water Gate (Nehemiah 8).
The people build booths in the square of the Water Gate for the Feast of Booths (Nehemiah 8).

name: Ariel
what: A poetic name for Jerusalem, the city where David camped.
today: Jerusalem.
key: Isaiah pronounces woe on Ariel, the city where David encamped (Isaiah 29).
God will bring distress on Ariel, and it will be like an altar hearth (Isaiah 29).
The nations fighting against Ariel will vanish like a dream (Isaiah 29).

name: Fish Gate
what: A gate in Jerusalem's northern wall, probably named for the fish market nearby.
today: Exact site unknown; on the north side of ancient Jerusalem.
key: Manasseh built an outer wall for Jerusalem around to the Fish Gate (2 Chronicles 33).
The sons of Hassenaah rebuilt the Fish Gate with its beams, doors, and bars (Nehemiah 3).
Zephaniah warns that a cry will rise from the Fish Gate on the day of the LORD (Zephaniah 1).

name: Fountain Gate
what: A gate at the southeast corner of Jerusalem's wall, near the Pool of Siloam.
today: Exact site unknown; near the southern end of the City of David, Jerusalem.
key: During his night inspection, Nehemiah reached the Fountain Gate but could not pass through (Nehemiah 2).
Shallun rebuilt the Fountain Gate and the wall of the Pool of Shelah (Nehemiah 3).
At the wall's dedication, a procession went up by the Fountain Gate to the City of David (Nehemiah 12).

name: Golgotha
what: The place just outside Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified, meaning Place of a Skull.
today: Traditionally at the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem.
key: Soldiers brought Jesus to Golgotha and offered him wine mixed with gall (Matthew 27).
Mark explains that Golgotha means Place of a Skull, where Jesus was crucified (Mark 15).
Jesus carried his own cross to Golgotha, where he was crucified between two others (John 19).

name: Siloam
what: An area and pool at the southern end of ancient Jerusalem, fed by the Gihon spring.
today: Pool remains excavated in the City of David, south of Jerusalem's Old City.
key: Jesus asked whether eighteen killed when the tower in Siloam fell were worse sinners (Luke 13).
Jesus sent a man born blind to wash in the pool of Siloam, and he came back seeing (John 9).

name: Bethesda
what: A pool in Jerusalem near the Sheep Gate, surrounded by covered colonnades where the sick lay.
today: The Pools of Bethesda, near St. Anne's Church in the Old City of Jerusalem.
key: The pool by the Sheep Gate had five roofed colonnades filled with sick and disabled people (John 5).
Jesus healed a man who had been disabled for thirty-eight years and told him to walk (John 5).
Because the healing happened on the Sabbath, Jewish leaders began to persecute Jesus (John 5).

name: Gethsemane
what: A garden or olive grove on the Mount of Olives where Jesus prayed and was arrested.
today: At the foot of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley from Jerusalem's Old City.
key: Jesus prayed in anguish at Gethsemane, submitting to his Father's will (Matthew 26).
Judas arrived with an armed crowd, identified Jesus with a kiss, and Jesus was arrested (Matthew 26).
Jesus found Peter, James, and John sleeping three times while he prayed (Mark 14).
John notes the garden lay across the Kidron, where Jesus often met with his disciples (John 18).

name: Jebusite
what: The ridge of the Jebusite city, Jerusalem, used as a landmark on Judah's northern boundary.
today: The City of David, south of the Old City of Jerusalem.
key: Judah's boundary ran up the Valley of Hinnom along the southern slope of the Jebusite city (Joshua 15).
The people of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem (Joshua 15).
Benjamin's border went down the Valley of Hinnom, south of the Jebusite slope (Joshua 18).
David captured the stronghold of Zion from the Jebusites (2 Samuel 5).

name: Hall of Judgment
what: A cedar-paneled hall in Solomon's palace complex where the king sat to give judgment.
today: Part of Solomon's palace in Jerusalem; it no longer exists.
key: Solomon made the Hall of the Throne, the Hall of Judgment, paneled with cedar from floor to rafters (1 Kings 7).
Solomon built a house for Pharaoh's daughter like this hall (1 Kings 7).

name: Perez-uzzah
what: The threshing floor where God struck Uzzah dead for touching the ark of the covenant.
today: Exact site unknown; between Kiriath-jearim and Jerusalem.
key: At Nacon's threshing floor Uzzah took hold of the ark, and God struck him down (2 Samuel 6).
David was angry and afraid, and named the place Perez-uzzah (2 Samuel 6).
Chronicles records the same event at the threshing floor of Chidon (1 Chronicles 13).

name: Place of a Skull
what: The place just outside Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified, the meaning of the name Golgotha.
today: Traditionally at the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem.
key: Soldiers brought Jesus to Golgotha, the Place of a Skull, and crucified him there (Matthew 27).
Mark explains that Golgotha means Place of a Skull, where Jesus was crucified (Mark 15).

name: Pool of Shelah
what: A pool by the king's garden in Jerusalem, likely the same as the Pool of Siloam.
today: Likely the Pool of Siloam area, City of David, south of Jerusalem's Old City.
key: Shallun rebuilt the Fountain Gate and the wall of the Pool of Shelah (Nehemiah 3).
The rebuilt wall ran past the king's garden to the stairs down from the City of David (Nehemiah 3).

name: Way of Holiness
what: A prophetic highway in Isaiah on which God's redeemed people return to Zion.
today: A prophetic image, not a known physical road.
key: Isaiah foresees a highway through the desert called the Way of Holiness (Isaiah 35).
The unclean will not travel it, and no lion or ravenous beast will be there (Isaiah 35).
The redeemed will walk it and return to Zion with singing and everlasting joy (Isaiah 35).

name: Second Quarter
what: A newer district of Jerusalem where the prophetess Huldah lived in Josiah's day.
today: Likely the western hill of Jerusalem's Old City.
key: Huldah the prophetess lived in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter (2 Kings 22).
Chronicles also places Huldah's home in the Second Quarter (2 Chronicles 34).
Zephaniah foretold a wail from the Second Quarter on the day of the LORD (Zephaniah 1).

name: Tower of the Ovens
what: A tower on Jerusalem's wall, repaired in Nehemiah's day and passed by a choir at the wall's dedication.
today: Exact site unknown; on the western side of ancient Jerusalem
key: Malchijah son of Harim and Hasshub son of Pahath-moab repaired the Tower of the Ovens (Nehemiah 3).
At the wall's dedication, one thanksgiving choir passed the Tower of the Ovens to the Broad Wall (Nehemiah 12).

name: Valley Gate
what: A gate in Jerusalem's wall facing a valley, used by Nehemiah for his night inspection of the walls.
today: Possibly on the southwest side of the City of David, Jerusalem.
key: King Uzziah built fortified towers in Jerusalem at the Valley Gate (2 Chronicles 26).
Nehemiah went out by night through the Valley Gate to inspect the broken walls (Nehemiah 2).
Hanun and the people of Zanoah rebuilt it and set its doors, bolts, and bars (Nehemiah 3).

name: Ekron
what: The northernmost of the five main Philistine cities.
today: Tel Miqne, Israel
key: Ekron is listed among the five Philistine cities still unconquered (Joshua 13).
When the ark reached Ekron, its people cried out in panic (1 Samuel 5).
Israel chased the Philistines to Ekron after Goliath fell (1 Samuel 17).
King Ahaziah sent to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron (2 Kings 1).

name: Shephelah
what: The low rolling hills between Judah's hill country and the coastal plain.
today: The low hills between Israel's coastal plain and the Judean highlands.
key: Solomon made cedar as plentiful as sycamore trees of the Shephelah (1 Kings 10).
David appointed officials over the olive and sycamore trees of the Shephelah (1 Chronicles 27).
Uzziah kept large herds in the Shephelah and the plain (2 Chronicles 26).
The Philistines raided the cities of the Shephelah in Ahaz's reign (2 Chronicles 28).

name: Moriah
what: The land and mountain where God tested Abraham by asking him to offer Isaac.
today: Traditionally the Temple Mount area of Jerusalem.
key: God told Abraham to offer Isaac on a mountain in the land of Moriah (Genesis 22).
The angel of the Lord stopped Abraham, and God provided a ram in Isaac's place (Genesis 22).
Abraham named the place The Lord Will Provide (Genesis 22).

name: Mount Moriah
what: The hill in Jerusalem where Solomon built the temple, on the threshing floor of Ornan.
today: The Temple Mount in Jerusalem's Old City.
key: Abraham was sent to offer Isaac on a mountain in the land of Moriah (Genesis 22).
David bought Ornan's threshing floor and built an altar there to stop a plague (1 Chronicles 21).
Solomon began building the temple on Mount Moriah, where the Lord had appeared to David (2 Chronicles 3).

name: Mount of Olives
what: A ridge east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley.
today: The ridge facing the Old City of Jerusalem from the east.
key: David went up the Mount of Olives weeping as he fled from Absalom (2 Samuel 15).
Zechariah foresaw the Lord standing on the Mount of Olives as it splits in two (Zechariah 14).
Jesus began his entry into Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives (Matthew 21).
Seated on the Mount of Olives, Jesus taught about the end of the age (Matthew 24).
After the Last Supper, Jesus went to the Mount of Olives to pray (Luke 22).

name: Olivet
what: The Mount of Olives, a ridge east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley.
today: The Mount of Olives, east of the Old City of Jerusalem.
key: Jesus approached Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet and sent for a colt (Luke 19).
During his final week Jesus taught in the temple and lodged nightly on Olivet (Luke 21).
After Jesus ascended, the apostles returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet (Acts 1).

name: Mount of Olives
what: A ridge east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley.
today: The ridge facing the Old City of Jerusalem from the east.
key: David went up the Mount of Olives weeping as he fled from Absalom (2 Samuel 15).
Zechariah foresaw the Lord standing on the Mount of Olives as it splits in two (Zechariah 14).
Seated on the Mount of Olives, Jesus taught about the end of the age (Matthew 24).
After the Last Supper, Jesus went to the Mount of Olives to pray (Luke 22).
Jesus ascended to heaven from the Mount of Olives (Acts 1).

name: Eshtaol
what: A town in the Shephelah near Zorah, linked with Samson.
today: Exact site uncertain; near modern Eshtaol, west of Jerusalem.
key: Eshtaol was allotted to Dan (Joshua 19).
The Spirit of the Lord began to stir Samson between Zorah and Eshtaol (Judges 13).
Samson was buried between Zorah and Eshtaol (Judges 16).
The Danites sent warriors from Zorah and Eshtaol to take new land (Judges 18).

name: Timnah
what: A town in the Sorek Valley on the border between Judah and Philistine territory.
today: Likely Tel Batash in the Sorek Valley, Israel.
key: Judah went up to Timnah to shear his sheep and met Tamar on the way (Genesis 38).
Timnah lay on Judah's northern boundary (Joshua 15).
Samson married a Philistine woman from Timnah and killed a lion nearby (Judges 14).
The Philistines captured Timnah during Ahaz's reign (2 Chronicles 28).

name: Bethphage
what: A village on the Mount of Olives near Bethany, just east of Jerusalem.
today: Likely on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, near modern et-Tur.
key: Near Bethphage, Jesus sent two disciples to bring a donkey and her colt (Matthew 21).
Mark records Jesus nearing Bethphage and Bethany before entering Jerusalem (Mark 11).
From near Bethphage Jesus began his royal entry as disciples praised God (Luke 19).

name: Nob
what: A town of priests in Benjamin just north of Jerusalem, where the tabernacle stood in Saul's day.
today: Exact site uncertain; likely near Mount Scopus, north of Jerusalem.
key: Ahimelech the priest gave David holy bread and Goliath's sword at Nob (1 Samuel 21).
Saul had Doeg kill the priests of Nob and strike the town (1 Samuel 22).
Benjaminites resettled Nob after the exile (Nehemiah 11).
Isaiah pictured the Assyrian halting at Nob to shake his fist at Zion (Isaiah 10).

name: Heshbon
what: A city east of the Jordan, the capital of Sihon king of the Amorites.
today: Tell Hesban, Jordan
key: Israel defeated Sihon and took Heshbon, his royal city (Numbers 21).
Moses gave Heshbon to the tribe of Reuben (Joshua 13).
Heshbon was assigned to the Levites (Joshua 21).
Isaiah lamented over Heshbon in his oracle against Moab (Isaiah 15).

name: Reuben
what: The tribal territory of Reuben on the plateau east of the Dead Sea.
today: Central Jordan, north of Wadi Mujib and east of the Dead Sea.
key: Reuben and Gad asked Moses for land east of the Jordan because of their livestock (Numbers 32).
Moses gave Reuben land from Aroer on the Arnon, including Heshbon and Dibon (Joshua 13).
Reuben gave the Levites four cities, including Bezer (Joshua 21).

name: Ashdod
what: One of the five main Philistine cities, near the Mediterranean coast.
today: Tel Ashdod, near Ashdod, Israel
key: Some of the Anakim remained in Ashdod after Joshua's campaigns (Joshua 11).
The captured ark was placed in Dagon's temple in Ashdod, and Dagon fell (1 Samuel 5).
King Uzziah broke down the wall of Ashdod (2 Chronicles 26).
Isaiah walked barefoot as a sign when the Assyrians captured Ashdod (Isaiah 20).
Nehemiah rebuked Jews whose children spoke the language of Ashdod (Nehemiah 13).

name: Ashan
what: A town in the lowland of Judah, later allotted to Simeon and given to the priests.
today: Exact site uncertain; possibly near Beersheba, southern Israel.
key: Ashan is listed among the towns of the lowland of Judah (Joshua 15).
Ashan is allotted to the tribe of Simeon (Joshua 19).
Ashan appears among the towns where Simeon's descendants lived (1 Chronicles 4).
Ashan is given with its pasturelands to the descendants of Aaron (1 Chronicles 6).

name: Anathoth
what: A Levitical town in Benjamin just northeast of Jerusalem, the hometown of Jeremiah.
today: Likely near Anata, northeast of Jerusalem, West Bank
key: Anathoth was given to the priests as a Levitical city (Joshua 21).
Solomon banished the priest Abiathar to his estate at Anathoth (1 Kings 2).
Jeremiah was from the priests of Anathoth (Jeremiah 1).
Men of Anathoth plotted to kill Jeremiah (Jeremiah 11).
Jeremiah bought a field at Anathoth as a sign of future restoration (Jeremiah 32).

name: Elealeh
what: A town on the plateau east of the Jordan, near Heshbon.
today: El-'Al, north of Heshbon in Jordan.
key: The Reubenites rebuilt Elealeh (Numbers 32).
Isaiah pictured Heshbon and Elealeh crying out (Isaiah 15).
Isaiah wept for Heshbon and Elealeh as their harvest failed (Isaiah 16).
Jeremiah heard Moab's cry from Heshbon to Elealeh (Jeremiah 48).

name: Sibmah
what: A town on the plateau east of the Dead Sea, famed for its vineyards.
today: Exact site unknown; near Heshbon in Jordan.
key: The Reubenites rebuilt Sibmah (Numbers 32).
Sibmah was allotted to Reuben (Joshua 13).
Isaiah mourned the ruined vines of Sibmah (Isaiah 16).
Jeremiah wept for the vine of Sibmah (Jeremiah 48).

name: Gallim
what: A town in Benjamin north of Jerusalem, home of Palti, who was given David's wife Michal.
today: Exact site unknown; north of Jerusalem.
key: Saul gave his daughter Michal, David's wife, to Palti son of Laish, of Gallim (1 Samuel 25).
Isaiah calls the daughter of Gallim to cry aloud as the Assyrian army advances (Isaiah 10).

name: Debir
what: A landmark on Judah's northern boundary near the Valley of Achor; not the Debir captured by Othniel.
today: Exact site unknown; likely between Jerusalem and Jericho, West Bank.
key: Judah's northern boundary went up to Debir from the Valley of Achor (Joshua 15).
From there the border turned north toward Gilgal, opposite the ascent of Adummim (Joshua 15).

name: Adummim
what: An ascent on the road from Jericho up to Jerusalem, on the boundary between Judah and Benjamin.
today: Likely Tal'at ed-Damm, near Ma'ale Adummim east of Jerusalem
key: Judah's northern border turned toward Gilgal, opposite the ascent of Adummim (Joshua 15).
Benjamin's southern border also ran opposite the ascent of Adummim (Joshua 18).

name: Gederah
what: A town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah.
today: Exact site uncertain; in the Shephelah of Judah.
key: Gederah is listed among the towns of Judah's lowland (Joshua 15).
Potters who worked for the king lived at Netaim and Gederah (1 Chronicles 4).
Jozabad of Gederah joined David's mighty men at Ziklag (1 Chronicles 12).

name: Netaim
what: A village of Judah where potters in the king's service lived.
today: Exact site unknown; likely in the lowland of Judah.
key: Potters who worked for the king lived at Netaim and Gederah (1 Chronicles 4).
These potters belonged to the clans descended from Shelah son of Judah (1 Chronicles 4).

name: Gedor
what: A place in the south where Simeonite clans found rich pasture in King Hezekiah's day.
today: Exact site unknown.
key: Simeonite clans went to the entrance of Gedor, east of the valley, to seek pasture for their flocks (1 Chronicles 4).
They found rich, good pasture in a land that was very broad, quiet, and peaceful (1 Chronicles 4).
In Hezekiah's days they struck down the Meunim there and settled in their place (1 Chronicles 4).

name: Gibeah
what: A town of Benjamin north of Jerusalem, King Saul's hometown and capital.
today: Likely Tell el-Ful, on Jerusalem's northern edge
key: Men of Gibeah abused and killed a Levite's concubine (Judges 19).
Israel's tribes went to war against Gibeah and Benjamin (Judges 20).
Saul returned home to Gibeah after being chosen king (1 Samuel 10).
Seven of Saul's descendants were put to death at Gibeah of Saul (2 Samuel 21).

name: Bahurim
what: A village in Benjamin just east of the Mount of Olives, on the road toward the Jordan.
today: Possibly Ras et-Tmim, east of Jerusalem.
key: Paltiel followed Michal weeping as far as Bahurim (2 Samuel 3).
Shimei came out from Bahurim cursing David as he fled Absalom (2 Samuel 16).
Jonathan and Ahimaaz hid in a well at Bahurim (2 Samuel 17).
Shimei hurried from Bahurim to meet David and beg forgiveness (2 Samuel 19).
David warned Solomon about Shimei of Bahurim (1 Kings 2).

name: Valley of Sorek
what: A broad valley running west from the hills of Judah into Philistine territory.
today: Nahal Sorek, west of Jerusalem toward the coast, Israel.
key: Samson loved Delilah, who lived in the Valley of Sorek (Judges 16).
The Philistine lords paid Delilah to learn the secret of Samson's strength, and she betrayed him (Judges 16).

name: Mizpah
what: A town of Benjamin north of Jerusalem where Israel often assembled.
today: Likely Tell en-Nasbeh, north of Jerusalem, West Bank
key: Israel gathered at Mizpah before going to war against Benjamin (Judges 20).
Samuel led Israel in repentance at Mizpah, and God routed the Philistines (1 Samuel 7).
Saul was chosen king by lot at Mizpah (1 Samuel 10).
King Asa built up Mizpah with stones taken from Ramah (2 Chronicles 16).
Gedaliah governed Judah from Mizpah until Ishmael murdered him (Jeremiah 41).

name: Ramah
what: The hometown of Samuel's family in the hill country of Ephraim and Benjamin.
today: Exact site uncertain; possibly er-Ram or Nebi Samwil, just north of Jerusalem.
key: Elkanah and Hannah lived in Ramah, where Samuel was born (1 Samuel 1).
Samuel judged Israel from his home in Ramah and built an altar there (1 Samuel 7).
Israel's elders came to Samuel at Ramah and asked for a king (1 Samuel 8).
David fled from Saul to Samuel at Ramah (1 Samuel 19).
Samuel died and was buried in his house at Ramah (1 Samuel 25).

name: Naioth
what: A place in Ramah where Samuel lived with a company of prophets.
today: Exact site unknown; at Ramah, likely north of Jerusalem.
key: David fled to Samuel at Naioth, and Saul's men and Saul himself prophesied there (1 Samuel 19).
David fled from Naioth to ask Jonathan why Saul sought his life (1 Samuel 20).

name: Arimathea
what: A town of Judea, home of Joseph, the disciple who buried Jesus.
today: Exact site uncertain; possibly Rentis, northwest of Jerusalem.
key: Joseph of Arimathea, a rich disciple, lays Jesus' body in his own new tomb (Matthew 27).
Joseph, a respected council member, boldly asks Pilate for Jesus' body (Mark 15).
Joseph, a secret disciple, and Nicodemus prepare and bury Jesus' body (John 19).

name: Ebenezer
what: A place near Aphek where Israel lost the ark to the Philistines, and later a memorial stone.
today: Exact site uncertain; possibly Izbet Sartah, near Aphek east of Tel Aviv.
key: Israel camped at Ebenezer and was defeated by the Philistines, who captured the ark (1 Samuel 4).
The Philistines carried the ark from Ebenezer to Ashdod (1 Samuel 5).
After victory, Samuel set up a stone named Ebenezer, saying the LORD had helped them (1 Samuel 7).

name: Ramathaim-zophim
what: A town in the hill country of Ephraim, home of Elkanah and Hannah and birthplace of Samuel.
today: Exact site debated; often linked with Ramah north of Jerusalem.
key: Elkanah, husband of Hannah, was from Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim (1 Samuel 1).
After praying at Shiloh, Hannah returned home to Ramah and gave birth to Samuel (1 Samuel 1).
Samuel made Ramah his home, judged Israel there, and built an altar to the Lord (1 Samuel 7).

name: Chephirah
what: One of four Gibeonite cities that made a treaty with Joshua, later part of Benjamin.
today: Khirbet el-Kefireh, west of Jerusalem, Israel.
key: Chephirah is one of the Gibeonite cities spared through Israel's treaty (Joshua 9).
Chephirah is allotted to the tribe of Benjamin (Joshua 18).
Men of Chephirah return from exile in Babylon (Ezra 2).
The returnees from Chephirah are listed again (Nehemiah 7).

name: Valley of Achor
what: A valley near Jericho where Achan was executed, later named in prophecy as a place of hope.
today: Possibly el-Buqei'a, west of the northern Dead Sea.
key: Achan and his household are stoned in the Valley of Achor for taking devoted things (Joshua 7).
The Valley of Achor marks part of Judah's northern boundary (Joshua 15).
God promises the Valley of Achor will become a resting place for herds (Isaiah 65).
God promises to make the Valley of Achor a door of hope for Israel (Hosea 2).

name: Beth-hoglah
what: A border town near the Jordan River between the territories of Judah and Benjamin.
today: Likely near Ein Hajla, southeast of Jericho.
key: Judah's northern boundary went up to Beth-hoglah from the mouth of the Jordan (Joshua 15).
Beth-hoglah is named on Benjamin's border and among Benjamin's towns (Joshua 18).

name: Emmaus
what: A village about seven miles from Jerusalem where the risen Jesus was recognized by two disciples.
today: Exact site unknown; several villages west of Jerusalem have been proposed.
key: The risen Jesus joined two disciples walking to Emmaus, but they did not recognize him (Luke 24).
He explained how all the Scriptures spoke of the Christ's suffering and glory (Luke 24).
They recognized Jesus when he broke bread, and he vanished from their sight (Luke 24).
The two hurried back to Jerusalem to tell the eleven that the Lord had risen (Luke 24).

name: Aijalon
what: A town in the Shephelah guarding the Aijalon Valley route to Jerusalem.
today: Near the village of Yalo, close to Latrun, west of Jerusalem.
key: Aijalon was allotted to Dan and given to the Levites (Joshua 21).
The Amorites persisted in living in Aijalon (Judges 1).
Israel struck the Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon (1 Samuel 14).
Rehoboam fortified Aijalon (2 Chronicles 11).
The Philistines captured Aijalon during Ahaz's reign (2 Chronicles 28).

name: Beth-arabah
what: A town in the Jordan Valley on the border between Judah and Benjamin.
today: Exact site uncertain; likely near the Jordan River southeast of Jericho.
key: Beth-arabah lies on Judah's northern boundary and is listed among Judah's wilderness towns (Joshua 15).
Beth-arabah also appears among the towns allotted to the tribe of Benjamin (Joshua 18).

name: Gibeon
what: A Hivite city northwest of Jerusalem that made a treaty with Israel by deception.
today: El-Jib, northwest of Jerusalem, West Bank
key: The Gibeonites tricked Joshua into making a peace treaty (Joshua 9).
The sun stood still while Joshua defended Gibeon against five kings (Joshua 10).
David's and Ish-bosheth's men fought beside the pool of Gibeon (2 Samuel 2).
God appeared to Solomon in a dream at Gibeon and offered him wisdom (1 Kings 3).
The tabernacle remained at the high place at Gibeon (1 Chronicles 16).

name: Geba
what: The starting point of David's rout of the Philistines; Chronicles names Gibeon in the same account.
today: Possibly Gibeon (el-Jib), northwest of Jerusalem, West Bank.
key: When the Philistines came up to the Valley of Rephaim again, God told David to circle behind them (2 Samuel 5).
David struck down the Philistines from Geba to Gezer (2 Samuel 5).
Chronicles records the same victory as from Gibeon to Gezer (1 Chronicles 14).

name: Mephaath
what: A town on the tableland of Moab, allotted to Reuben and given to the Levites.
today: Likely Umm er-Rasas, southeast of Madaba, Jordan.
key: Mephaath is allotted to the tribe of Reuben (Joshua 13).
Mephaath is given to the Merarite Levites (Joshua 21).
Mephaath is listed again among the Levitical cities (1 Chronicles 6).
Jeremiah names Mephaath among Moab's cities facing judgment (Jeremiah 48).

name: Benjamin
what: The tribal territory allotted to Benjamin, a narrow strip of hill country between Judah and Ephraim.
today: The central hills north of Jerusalem, mostly in the West Bank.
key: After the land was surveyed from Shiloh, Benjamin's lot came up between Judah and the sons of Joseph (Joshua 18).
Its boundaries ran from the Jordan near Jericho westward past Bethel and Kiriath-jearim (Joshua 18).
Its towns included Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon, Ramah, and Jebus, which is Jerusalem (Joshua 18).

name: Geba
what: A Levitical town in Benjamin north of Jerusalem, often marking the northern edge of Judah.
today: The village of Jaba, about 9 km north-northeast of Jerusalem.
key: Geba was given to the priests as a Levitical city from Benjamin (Joshua 21).
Jonathan defeated the Philistine garrison at Geba, provoking war with the Philistines (1 Samuel 13).
King Asa built up Geba using stones Baasha had used to fortify Ramah (1 Kings 15).
Josiah defiled the high places from Geba to Beersheba (2 Kings 23).
Zechariah foresaw the land from Geba to Rimmon becoming a plain (Zechariah 14).

name: Shittim
what: Israel's final camp on the plains of Moab before crossing the Jordan.
today: Possibly Tell el-Hammam, east of the Jordan opposite Jericho, Jordan.
key: While at Shittim, Israel commits sexual immorality with Moabite women and worships Baal (Numbers 25).
Joshua secretly sends two spies from Shittim to Jericho (Joshua 2).
Israel sets out from Shittim and comes to the Jordan (Joshua 3).
Micah calls Israel to remember what happened from Shittim to Gilgal (Micah 6).

name: Abel-shittim
what: Israel's final camp on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan opposite Jericho.
today: Possibly Tell el-Hammam, east of the Jordan opposite Jericho, Jordan.
key: While camped at Shittim, Israel worshiped Baal of Peor with Moabite women, and a plague followed (Numbers 25).
Israel camped along the Jordan from Beth-jeshimoth to Abel-shittim in the plains of Moab (Numbers 33).
Joshua secretly sent two spies from Shittim to scout Jericho (Joshua 2).

name: Gilgal
what: Israel's first camp west of the Jordan near Jericho, later a place of worship and assembly.
today: Near Jericho, West Bank; exact site unknown
key: Joshua set up twelve stones from the Jordan at Gilgal (Joshua 4).
Israel was circumcised and kept the Passover at Gilgal, and the manna ceased (Joshua 5).
The people made Saul king before the LORD at Gilgal (1 Samuel 11).
Saul offered a burnt offering at Gilgal without waiting for Samuel (1 Samuel 13).
Samuel rebuked Saul at Gilgal for sparing Agag and the Amalekite spoil (1 Samuel 15).

name: Michmash
what: A town in Benjamin across a steep ravine from Geba, north of Jerusalem.
today: The village of Mukhmas, northeast of Jerusalem in the West Bank.
key: The Philistines encamped at Michmash with a huge army against Saul (1 Samuel 13).
Jonathan and his armor-bearer attacked the Philistine garrison at the pass of Michmash (1 Samuel 14).
Men of Benjamin resettled Michmash after the exile (Nehemiah 11).
Isaiah pictured the Assyrian army storing its baggage at Michmash (Isaiah 10).

name: Jericho
what: An ancient oasis city near the Jordan River, the first city Israel conquered in Canaan.
today: Tell es-Sultan, near Jericho, West Bank
key: Rahab hid the two Israelite spies in Jericho (Joshua 2).
The walls fell after Israel marched around the city for seven days (Joshua 6).
Hiel rebuilt Jericho at the cost of his sons, as Joshua had warned (1 Kings 16).
Elisha healed Jericho's bad spring with a bowl of salt (2 Kings 2).
Jesus called Zacchaeus down from a tree in Jericho (Luke 19).

name: Gezer
what: A strategic Canaanite city guarding the route from the coastal plain up to Jerusalem.
today: Tel Gezer, between Jerusalem and Tel Aviv near Ramla.
key: Horam king of Gezer came to help Lachish, and Joshua struck him down (Joshua 10).
Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer (Joshua 16).
David struck down the Philistines from Geba to Gezer (2 Samuel 5).
Pharaoh captured Gezer and gave it as a dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife, and Solomon rebuilt it (1 Kings 9).
Sibbecai killed a descendant of the giants in a battle with the Philistines at Gezer (1 Chronicles 20).

name: Gob
what: A battle site where David's men fought the Philistines and killed descendants of the giants.
today: Exact site unknown.
key: At Gob, Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Saph, a descendant of the giants (2 Samuel 21).
In another battle at Gob, Elhanan of Bethlehem struck down a Philistine giant (2 Samuel 21).

name: Beth-horon
what: Twin towns guarding a key pass from the coastal plain up to the hill country.
today: Beit Ur al-Fauqa and Beit Ur al-Tahta, northwest of Jerusalem in the West Bank.
key: Israel chased the Amorites down the descent of Beth-horon (Joshua 10).
Beth-horon lay on the boundary between Benjamin and Ephraim (Joshua 18).
Beth-horon was given to the Levites from Ephraim (Joshua 21).
A company of Philistine raiders went out toward Beth-horon (1 Samuel 13).
Dismissed Israelite troops raided Judah's cities from Samaria to Beth-horon (2 Chronicles 25).

name: Lower Beth-horon
what: The lower of two towns guarding the ascent from the coastal plain toward the hill country northwest of Jerusalem.
today: Beit Ur et-Tahta, northwest of Jerusalem, West Bank.
key: Lower Beth-horon marks the boundary of the descendants of Joseph (Joshua 16).
Lower Beth-horon lies on the border of Benjamin's territory (Joshua 18).
Solomon rebuilds Lower Beth-horon (1 Kings 9).
Solomon fortifies Upper and Lower Beth-horon with walls, gates, and bars (2 Chronicles 8).

name: Beth-aven
what: A place near Bethel and Ai; Hosea also uses the name for idolatrous Bethel.
today: Exact site unknown; near Bethel, north of Jerusalem in the West Bank.
key: Joshua sent spies to Ai, near Beth-aven, east of Bethel (Joshua 7).
The Philistines encamped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven (1 Samuel 13).
After Jonathan's attack, the battle passed beyond Beth-aven (1 Samuel 14).
Hosea warned Israel not to go up to Beth-aven to worship (Hosea 4).
Hosea said the people would mourn over the calf idol of Beth-aven (Hosea 10).

name: Ramah
what: A town of Benjamin north of Jerusalem, near the border with the northern kingdom.
today: Er-Ram, north of Jerusalem, West Bank
key: Deborah judged Israel between Ramah and Bethel (Judges 4).
King Baasha of Israel fortified Ramah to block access to Judah (1 Kings 15).
Jeremiah described Rachel weeping for her children in Ramah (Jeremiah 31).
Jeremiah was released from his chains at Ramah after Jerusalem fell (Jeremiah 40).

name: Bezek
what: The place where Judah and Simeon defeated the Canaanites and Perizzites and captured Adoni-bezek.
today: Exact site unknown; possibly Khirbet Bezqa near Gezer
key: After Joshua's death, Judah and Simeon defeated ten thousand Canaanites and Perizzites at Bezek (Judges 1).
They fought Adoni-bezek there, pursued him, and cut off his thumbs and big toes (Judges 1).

name: Beeroth
what: One of the four Gibeonite cities, later part of the tribe of Benjamin.
today: Possibly el-Bireh, near Ramallah in the West Bank.
key: Beeroth was one of the Gibeonite cities that made peace with Israel (Joshua 9).
It was allotted to the tribe of Benjamin (Joshua 18).
Rechab and Baanah of Beeroth murdered Ish-bosheth (2 Samuel 4).
Naharai of Beeroth was Joab's armor-bearer among David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23).
Men of Beeroth returned from exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2).

name: Beer
what: A place where Jotham fled after proclaiming his fable against his brother Abimelech.
today: Exact site unknown.
key: From Mount Gerizim Jotham told his parable of the trees against Abimelech and Shechem (Judges 9).
He then fled to Beer and lived there for fear of his brother Abimelech (Judges 9).

name: Mount Zemaraim
what: A hill in the hill country of Ephraim where King Abijah of Judah addressed Jeroboam's army.
today: Exact site unknown; in the hill country near Bethel, West Bank.
key: Abijah stood on Mount Zemaraim and rebuked Jeroboam and Israel for forsaking the Lord (2 Chronicles 13).
Though Jeroboam ambushed Judah, God gave Abijah's army victory over Israel (2 Chronicles 13).

name: Ai
what: A Canaanite town near Bethel, where Israel was defeated before capturing it.
today: Possibly et-Tell or Khirbet el-Maqatir, near Bethel, West Bank
key: Abram pitched his tent between Bethel and Ai (Genesis 12).
Israel was routed at Ai because Achan had taken devoted things (Joshua 7).
Joshua captured and burned Ai using an ambush (Joshua 8).
Men of Bethel and Ai returned from exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2).

name: Bethel
what: A town north of Jerusalem where God met Jacob, later a center of idolatrous worship in Israel.
today: Likely Beitin, north of Jerusalem, West Bank
key: Abram built an altar between Bethel and Ai (Genesis 12).
Jacob dreamed of a ladder to heaven and named the place Bethel (Genesis 28).
Jeroboam set up a golden calf at Bethel for the northern tribes (1 Kings 12).
Josiah tore down the altar at Bethel, fulfilling an earlier prophecy (2 Kings 23).
Amaziah the priest of Bethel ordered Amos to leave (Amos 7).

name: Luz
what: The original Canaanite name of Bethel, a town north of Jerusalem.
today: Bethel, likely Beitin near Ramallah in the West Bank.
key: After his dream, Jacob renamed the city of Luz Bethel (Genesis 28).
Jacob returned to Luz and built an altar there (Genesis 35).
Jacob told Joseph that God Almighty appeared to him at Luz (Genesis 48).
The house of Joseph captured Luz, and a spared man built another Luz elsewhere (Judges 1).

name: Bochim
what: The place where Israel wept after the angel of the Lord rebuked them for disobedience.
today: Exact site unknown; possibly near Bethel, West Bank.
key: The angel of the Lord came from Gilgal to Bochim and rebuked Israel for making covenants with Canaanites (Judges 2).
The people wept aloud, named the place Bochim, and offered sacrifices to the Lord (Judges 2).

name: Rimmon
what: A rocky stronghold in Benjamin where survivors of the tribe took refuge.
today: Likely near the village of Rammun, east of Bethel.
key: After the battle at Gibeah, six hundred Benjaminites fled to the rock of Rimmon (Judges 20).
Israel sent word of peace to the Benjaminites at the rock of Rimmon (Judges 21).

name: Makkedah
what: A Canaanite town in the Shephelah where five Amorite kings hid in a cave.
today: Exact site uncertain; in the Shephelah lowlands of Judah.
key: Five fleeing Amorite kings hid in a cave at Makkedah and were executed (Joshua 10).
Joshua captured Makkedah and struck down its king (Joshua 10).
Makkedah was allotted to Judah (Joshua 15).

name: Jazer
what: An Amorite town in Gilead east of the Jordan, known for its pastureland and vineyards.
today: Exact site uncertain; in Gilead, west of Amman, Jordan.
key: Israel captured Jazer and its villages from the Amorites (Numbers 21).
Gad and Reuben saw that the land of Jazer was good for livestock (Numbers 32).
Jazer was given to the Levites as a city in Gad (Joshua 21).
David's census officers passed through Jazer (2 Samuel 24).
Isaiah pictured Jazer weeping over the ruined vines of Moab (Isaiah 16).

name: Rabbah
what: The capital city of the Ammonites, east of the Jordan.
today: Amman, the capital of Jordan.
key: The iron bed of Og king of Bashan was kept in Rabbah (Deuteronomy 3).
While Joab besieged Rabbah, David sinned with Bathsheba and had Uriah killed (2 Samuel 11).
David captured Rabbah and took the crown from its king's head (2 Samuel 12).
Shobi of Rabbah brought supplies to David at Mahanaim during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 17).
Prophets announced that Rabbah would be destroyed in judgment (Amos 1).

name: Ammon
what: A nation east of the Jordan descended from Lot, often hostile to Israel.
today: The region around Amman in central Jordan.
key: God told Israel not to harass the Ammonites, since he had given their land to Lot's descendants (Deuteronomy 2).
Jephthah defeated the Ammonites after they oppressed Israel (Judges 11).
Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir attacked Judah but destroyed one another (2 Chronicles 20).
Nehemiah enforced the law excluding Ammonites from God's assembly (Nehemiah 13).
Ezekiel announced judgment on Ammon for rejoicing over Jerusalem's fall (Ezekiel 25).

name: The East
what: The desert lands east of the Jordan, home of nomadic tribes the Bible calls the people of the East.
today: The Syrian-Arabian desert east of Jordan; not a single site.
key: The people of the East joined Midian and Amalek in raiding Israel's crops (Judges 6).
Their camp lay in the valley like locusts in number before Gideon attacked (Judges 7).
Gideon's pursuit left 120,000 of the people of the East fallen (Judges 8).
Ezekiel foretold that Ammon and Moab would be handed over to the people of the East (Ezekiel 25).

name: Lod
what: A town on the coastal plain of Benjamin, resettled by returning exiles.
today: Lod, near Ben Gurion Airport, Israel.
key: Shemed of Benjamin builds Ono and Lod (1 Chronicles 8).
People of Lod, Hadid, and Ono return from exile (Ezra 2).
The returnees of Lod are listed again (Nehemiah 7).
Benjaminites live in Lod after the exile (Nehemiah 11).

name: Lud
what: A distant nation known for its archers and soldiers, listed among faraway peoples.
today: Uncertain; possibly Lydia in western Turkey, or a people in Africa.
key: God will send survivors to Lud and other nations to declare his glory (Isaiah 66).
Men of Lud, skilled archers, serve in Egypt's army (Jeremiah 46).
Men of Lud serve as soldiers in the army of Tyre (Ezekiel 27).
Lud is named among Egypt's allies who will fall by the sword (Ezekiel 30).

name: Lydda
what: A town on the coastal plain near Joppa, where Peter healed a paralyzed man.
today: Modern Lod, Israel, near Ben Gurion Airport.
key: At Lydda Peter healed Aeneas, bedridden eight years, and residents turned to the Lord (Acts 9).
Disciples from nearby Joppa sent to Lydda for Peter after Tabitha died (Acts 9).

name: Aroer
what: A town east of the Jordan near the Arnon River, on Israel's southern border with Moab.
today: Likely Khirbet 'Ara'ir on the Arnon in Jordan; another Aroer lay near Rabbah (Amman).
key: The tribe of Gad rebuilt Aroer (Numbers 32).
Aroer on the Arnon marked the southern edge of Reuben's territory (Joshua 13).
Jephthah struck the Ammonites from Aroer to Minnith (Judges 11).
David's census takers began at Aroer east of the Jordan (2 Samuel 24).
Isaiah foretold that the cities of Aroer would be deserted (Isaiah 17).

name: Hadid
what: A town near Lod in the lowlands, resettled by returning exiles.
today: Likely el-Haditheh, near Lod, Israel.
key: People of Lod, Hadid, and Ono were among those returning from Babylon (Ezra 2).
Nehemiah's list repeats the returnees from Lod, Hadid, and Ono (Nehemiah 7).
Members of the tribe of Benjamin settled in Hadid (Nehemiah 11).

name: Gibbethon
what: A town in Dan's territory near Philistine land, later contested with the Philistines.
today: Possibly Tel Malot, near Gezer, Israel.
key: Gibbethon was allotted to Dan (Joshua 19).
It was given to the Levites of Kohath's clan (Joshua 21).
Baasha killed King Nadab while Israel besieged Gibbethon (1 Kings 15).
The army at Gibbethon made Omri king after Zimri's coup (1 Kings 16).

name: Ephraim
what: The tribal territory of Ephraim in the central hill country of Canaan.
today: Central West Bank, around Shiloh and Bethel
key: Moses blessed Joseph's tribes, including the ten thousands of Ephraim (Deuteronomy 33).
Ephraim received its inheritance but did not drive out the Canaanites in Gezer (Joshua 16).
Joshua told Ephraim and Manasseh to clear the forested hill country (Joshua 17).
Joshua received Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim (Joshua 19).

name: Ono
what: A town near Lod in the coastal plain, settled by Benjamites after the exile.
today: Likely near modern Kiryat Ono, east of Tel Aviv, Israel.
key: Shemed of Benjamin built Ono and Lod (1 Chronicles 8).
People of Lod, Hadid, and Ono returned from exile (Ezra 2).
Sanballat and Geshem invited Nehemiah to the plain of Ono, intending harm (Nehemiah 6).
Benjaminites lived at Ono, in the valley of craftsmen (Nehemiah 11).

name: Arabah
what: The deep rift valley running from the Sea of Galilee through the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba.
today: Jordan Rift Valley, Israel and Jordan
key: Moses spoke to Israel beyond the Jordan in the Arabah (Deuteronomy 1).
Israel traveled along the Arabah road away from Edom (Deuteronomy 2).
The Dead Sea is called the Sea of the Arabah (Deuteronomy 3).
King Zedekiah fled toward the Arabah when Jerusalem fell (Jeremiah 52).

name: Gilead
what: A fertile, hilly region east of the Jordan River, settled by Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh.
today: Northwestern Jordan, east of the Jordan River
key: Jacob and Laban made a covenant in the hill country of Gilead (Genesis 31).
Reuben and Gad asked for Gilead because it suited their livestock (Numbers 32).
Jephthah the Gileadite led Israel against the Ammonites (Judges 11).
Elijah the Tishbite, from Gilead, announced a drought to Ahab (1 Kings 17).
Jeremiah lamented, asking whether there was no balm in Gilead (Jeremiah 8).

name: Havvoth-jair
what: A group of villages east of the Jordan, named after Jair of the tribe of Manasseh.
today: In Gilead and Bashan, northern Jordan; exact sites unknown.
key: Jair son of Manasseh captures villages and calls them Havvoth-jair (Numbers 32).
Jair takes the region of Argob and names Bashan's villages Havvoth-jair (Deuteronomy 3).
The judge Jair's thirty sons have thirty cities called Havvoth-jair in Gilead (Judges 10).
Geshur and Aram take Havvoth-jair from Israel (1 Chronicles 2).

name: Kamon
what: A town in Gilead where Jair, a judge of Israel, was buried.
today: Exact site unknown; in Gilead, in present-day northern Jordan.
key: Jair the Gileadite judged Israel twenty-two years, and his sons had thirty cities in Gilead (Judges 10).
Jair died and was buried in Kamon (Judges 10).

name: Gad
what: The tribal territory of Gad, east of the Jordan in the region of Gilead.
today: Western Jordan, east of the Jordan River
key: Gad and Reuben asked to settle east of the Jordan because of their livestock (Numbers 32).
Gad's fighting men crossed the Jordan to help conquer Canaan (Joshua 1).
Moses' allotment of land to the tribe of Gad is described (Joshua 13).
Hazael of Syria struck the land of Gad east of the Jordan (2 Kings 10).

name: Ezem
what: A town in the Negev of southern Judah, later counted among Simeon's towns.
today: Exact site unknown; in the Negev of southern Israel.
key: Ezem is listed among Judah's southernmost towns in the Negev (Joshua 15).
Ezem was included in the inheritance of Simeon within Judah's territory (Joshua 19).
The Chronicler names Ezem among the towns where Simeon's clans lived (1 Chronicles 4).

name: Bethel
what: A Canaanite royal city north of Jerusalem, near Ai, conquered by Joshua.
today: Likely Beitin, north of Jerusalem, West Bank.
key: Abram built an altar on a hill between Bethel and Ai (Genesis 12).
Jacob dreamed of a stairway to heaven and named the place Bethel (Genesis 28).
Joshua set an ambush between Bethel and Ai, and the men of Bethel joined the chase (Joshua 8).
The king of Bethel is listed among the kings Joshua defeated (Joshua 12).
Jeroboam set up a golden calf at Bethel for the northern tribes (1 Kings 12).

name: Joppa
what: An ancient port city on the Mediterranean coast of Israel.
today: Jaffa, the old port district of Tel Aviv-Yafo, Israel.
key: Hiram of Tyre floated cedar logs on rafts to Joppa for Solomon's temple (2 Chronicles 2).
Cedar for the second temple was again shipped to Joppa (Ezra 3).
Jonah went down to Joppa and boarded a ship for Tarshish to flee from the Lord (Jonah 1).
Peter raised Tabitha, also called Dorcas, from the dead in Joppa (Acts 9).
On a rooftop in Joppa, Peter received the vision preparing him to visit Cornelius (Acts 10).

name: Shiloh
what: A town in Ephraim where the tabernacle stood during the time of the judges.
today: Tel Shiloh (Khirbet Seilun), West Bank
key: Israel set up the tent of meeting at Shiloh, and Joshua cast lots for the land (Joshua 18).
Hannah prayed for a son at the house of the LORD in Shiloh (1 Samuel 1).
The LORD called the boy Samuel at Shiloh (1 Samuel 3).
The ark was taken from Shiloh into battle and captured by the Philistines (1 Samuel 4).
Jeremiah warned Judah to remember what God did to Shiloh (Jeremiah 7).

name: Gath-rimmon
what: A town on the coastal plain allotted to Dan and given to the Levites.
today: Exact site uncertain; possibly Tell Jerisheh near Tel Aviv.
key: Gath-rimmon is listed in the inheritance of the tribe of Dan (Joshua 19).
Gath-rimmon was given from Dan's land to the Kohathite Levites (Joshua 21).
The Chronicler lists Gath-rimmon among the Levites' towns (1 Chronicles 6).

name: Adam
what: A town in the Jordan Valley upstream from Jericho, where the Jordan's waters stopped for Israel's crossing.
today: Likely Tell ed-Damiyeh, near the Damiya Bridge over the Jordan, Jordan.
key: The Jordan's flood waters stood in a heap far upstream at Adam, the city beside Zarethan (Joshua 3).
With the waters cut off, Israel crossed on dry ground opposite Jericho (Joshua 3).

name: Aphek
what: A city on the Sharon plain where the Philistines gathered to fight Israel.
today: Tel Aphek, near Rosh HaAyin, central Israel.
key: The king of Aphek is listed among the kings Joshua defeated (Joshua 12).
The Philistines camp at Aphek and defeat Israel, then capture the ark (1 Samuel 4).
The Philistines gather at Aphek, and David is sent back from their army (1 Samuel 29).

name: Tappuah
what: A Canaanite town on the border between Ephraim and Manasseh.
today: Likely Sheikh Abu Zarad, south of Nablus.
key: The king of Tappuah was among the kings Joshua defeated (Joshua 12).
Ephraim's border went west from Tappuah to the brook Kanah (Joshua 16).
The land of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but the town itself belonged to Ephraim (Joshua 17).

name: Gaash
what: A mountain in the hill country of Ephraim near Joshua's burial place.
today: Exact site unknown; in the hill country of Ephraim, West Bank.
key: Joshua is buried at Timnath-serah, north of the mountain of Gaash (Joshua 24).
Judges repeats that Joshua was buried north of the mountain of Gaash (Judges 2).
Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash is among David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23).
Hurai of the brooks of Gaash appears in the list of David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 11).

name: Timnath-serah
what: Joshua's own town in the hill country of Ephraim, where he lived and was buried.
today: Likely Khirbet Tibnah, northwest of Bethel, West Bank.
key: Israel gave Joshua Timnath-serah at his request, and he rebuilt the town (Joshua 19).
Joshua was buried at Timnath-serah, north of the mountain of Gaash (Joshua 24).
Judges recalls his burial at Timnath-heres in the hill country of Ephraim (Judges 2).

name: Calno
what: A city in northern Syria conquered by Assyria, cited as a warning to Israel and Judah.
today: Likely Kullani (Tell Tayinat), near Antakya in southern Turkey.
key: Amos told Israel's complacent leaders to look at the fate of Calneh and Hamath (Amos 6).
Isaiah quoted Assyria boasting that Calno had fallen just like Carchemish (Isaiah 10).

name: Tel-abib
what: A settlement of Judean exiles by the Chebar canal in Babylonia, where Ezekiel lived.
today: Exact site unknown; by the Chebar canal near Nippur, southern Iraq.
key: Ezekiel came to the exiles at Tel-abib by the Chebar canal and sat overwhelmed seven days (Ezekiel 3).
After seven days, God appointed Ezekiel a watchman for the house of Israel (Ezekiel 3).

name: Kanah
what: A brook flowing west to the Mediterranean that formed part of the border between Ephraim and Manasseh.
today: Likely Wadi Qanah, which flows west into the Yarkon River, Israel and West Bank.
key: Ephraim's border went west from Tappuah to the brook Kanah and ended at the sea (Joshua 16).
Manasseh's boundary went down to the brook Kanah, though some towns south of it belonged to Ephraim (Joshua 17).

name: Tiphsah
what: A town that King Menahem of Israel attacked brutally because it would not open its gates.
today: Exact site uncertain; possibly Tappuah near Tirzah, West Bank.
key: Menahem seized Israel's throne by killing Shallum in Samaria (2 Kings 15).
He attacked Tiphsah brutally because it would not open its gates to him (2 Kings 15).

name: Penuel
what: A place by the Jabbok where Jacob saw God face to face, later a fortified town.
today: Likely Tell edh-Dhahab esh-Sharqi, on the Zarqa River in Jordan.
key: Jacob named the place Peniel, saying he had seen God face to face (Genesis 32).
Gideon tore down Penuel's tower after its men refused his army bread (Judges 8).
Jeroboam built up Penuel as a royal city (1 Kings 12).

name: Helam
what: A place east of the Jordan where David defeated the Syrian army allied with Ammon.
today: Exact site unknown; east of the Jordan, possibly Alma in southern Syria.
key: Hadadezer's Syrian forces gathered at Helam under his commander Shobach (2 Samuel 10).
David crossed the Jordan, defeated the Syrians at Helam, and Shobach died there (2 Samuel 10).

name: Karkor
what: A place in the desert east of the Jordan where Gideon routed the Midianite army.
today: Exact site unknown; east of the Jordan, possibly in Wadi Sirhan, Jordan.
key: Zebah and Zalmunna were at Karkor with about fifteen thousand men, all that remained of their army (Judges 8).
Gideon attacked the unsuspecting camp by the caravan route, routed it, and captured both kings (Judges 8).

name: Peniel
what: A place by the Jabbok River where Jacob wrestled with God and was renamed Israel.
today: Likely Tell edh-Dhahab esh-Sharqi, on the Zarqa (Jabbok) River in Jordan.
key: Jacob wrestled with a man until daybreak and was renamed Israel (Genesis 32).
Jacob named the place Peniel, saying he had seen God face to face (Genesis 32).
The sun rose as Jacob passed Penuel, limping because of his hip (Genesis 32).

name: Susa
what: A royal capital of the Persian Empire, with a fortified citadel.
today: Shush, southwestern Iran
key: Nehemiah was in the citadel of Susa when he heard of Jerusalem's ruin (Nehemiah 1).
King Ahasuerus reigned from Susa and held a great feast there (Esther 1).
Haman's decree to destroy the Jews was issued in Susa (Esther 3).
The Jews of Susa defended themselves against their enemies for two days (Esther 9).
Daniel saw a vision of a ram and a goat while in Susa (Daniel 8).

name: Elam
what: An ancient nation east of Babylonia whose capital region included Susa.
today: Southwestern Iran, around the modern province of Khuzestan.
key: Chedorlaomer king of Elam led a coalition of kings that captured Lot (Genesis 14).
Isaiah foresaw the Lord recovering a remnant of his people from Elam (Isaiah 11).
Elam and Media are summoned to besiege Babylon (Isaiah 21).
Jeremiah announced judgment on Elam but promised to restore its fortunes in the latter days (Jeremiah 49).
Daniel saw his vision of the ram and goat while at Susa in the province of Elam (Daniel 8).

name: Jabbok
what: A river flowing west into the Jordan, forming a natural boundary in the land of Gilead.
today: The Zarqa River in Jordan.
key: Jacob crossed the ford of the Jabbok and wrestled with a man until daybreak (Genesis 32).
Israel took Sihon's land from the Arnon to the Jabbok (Numbers 21).
Moses set the Jabbok as a border for Reuben and Gad (Deuteronomy 3).
Jephthah answered the Ammonite king's claim to the land between the Arnon and the Jabbok (Judges 11).

name: Mount Gerizim
what: A mountain beside Shechem, facing Mount Ebal, where the blessings of the covenant were pronounced.
today: Jabal at-Tur, above Nablus, West Bank.
key: Moses commands that the blessing be set on Mount Gerizim (Deuteronomy 11).
Six tribes are to stand on Mount Gerizim to bless the people (Deuteronomy 27).
Half of Israel stands before Mount Gerizim as Joshua reads the law (Joshua 8).
Jotham tells his fable of the trees from the top of Mount Gerizim (Judges 9).

name: Succoth
what: A town in the Jordan Valley east of the river, near the Jabbok.
today: Likely Tell Deir Alla in the Jordan Valley, Jordan.
key: Jacob built a house and shelters for his livestock and named the place Succoth (Genesis 33).
Succoth was allotted to the tribe of Gad (Joshua 13).
The officials of Succoth refused Gideon bread, and he later punished them (Judges 8).
Solomon's bronze temple furnishings were cast in clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan (1 Kings 7).

name: Shechem
what: An ancient city in the hill country of Ephraim, between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim.
today: Tell Balata, Nablus, West Bank
key: Abram built his first altar in Canaan at Shechem (Genesis 12).
Simeon and Levi killed the men of Shechem after Dinah was violated (Genesis 34).
Joshua renewed Israel's covenant at Shechem and Joseph's bones were buried there (Joshua 24).
Abimelech made himself king at Shechem and later destroyed the city (Judges 9).
Israel rejected Rehoboam at Shechem, and the kingdom divided (1 Kings 12).

name: Tower of Shechem
what: A fortified stronghold of Shechem, connected with the temple of El-berith.
today: Likely at Tell Balata, on the eastern edge of Nablus.
key: The leaders of the Tower of Shechem took refuge in the stronghold of the house of El-berith (Judges 9).
Abimelech set the stronghold on fire, and about a thousand people of the Tower of Shechem died (Judges 9).

name: Mahanaim
what: A town in Gilead east of the Jordan, near the Jabbok River.
today: Likely Tell edh-Dhahab el-Gharbi on the Jabbok River in Jordan.
key: Jacob met the angels of God here and named the place Mahanaim (Genesis 32).
It became a Levitical city in the territory of Gad (Joshua 21).
Abner made Saul's son Ish-bosheth king at Mahanaim (2 Samuel 2).
David took refuge at Mahanaim when fleeing from Absalom (2 Samuel 17).
Barzillai provided for David while he stayed at Mahanaim (2 Samuel 19).

name: Rogelim
what: A town in Gilead east of the Jordan, home of David's loyal supporter Barzillai.
today: Exact site unknown; in Gilead, northern Jordan.
key: Barzillai of Rogelim brought food and supplies to David at Mahanaim during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 17).
Barzillai came down from Rogelim to escort the king across the Jordan (2 Samuel 19).

name: Mount Ebal
what: A mountain north of Shechem, facing Mount Gerizim, where the covenant curses were proclaimed.
today: Mount Ebal, north of Nablus in the West Bank.
key: Moses commanded that the curse be set on Mount Ebal (Deuteronomy 11).
Israel was to build an altar and write the law on stones on Mount Ebal (Deuteronomy 27).
Joshua built the altar on Mount Ebal and read the whole law (Joshua 8).

name: Zeredah
what: A town in Ephraim, the hometown of Jeroboam, first king of the northern kingdom of Israel.
today: Exact site uncertain; possibly near Deir Ghassaneh in the hills of Samaria, West Bank.
key: Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite of Zeredah, rebelled against King Solomon (1 Kings 11).
The prophet Ahijah told Jeroboam that God would give him ten tribes (1 Kings 11).

name: Zarethan
what: A town in the Jordan Valley near Adam, where the Jordan's waters stopped for Israel's crossing.
today: Exact site unknown; possibly Tell es-Saidiyeh, east of the Jordan
key: The Jordan's waters stood in a heap at Adam, the city beside Zarethan, as Israel crossed (Joshua 3).
Baana's district under Solomon included Beth-shean, beside Zarethan (1 Kings 4).
Solomon's bronze temple furnishings were cast in clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan (1 Kings 7).

name: Tirzah
what: A Canaanite city that became the early capital of the northern kingdom of Israel.
today: Likely Tell el-Far'ah North, northeast of Nablus in the West Bank.
key: The king of Tirzah was among the kings Joshua defeated (Joshua 12).
Jeroboam's son died as his mother returned home to Tirzah (1 Kings 14).
Baasha reigned over Israel from Tirzah (1 Kings 15).
Zimri burned the palace over himself at Tirzah, and Omri later moved the capital to Samaria (1 Kings 16).
The bride in the Song is called beautiful as Tirzah (Song of Solomon 6).

name: Samaria
what: The capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, and later the hill region between Galilee and Judea.
today: Sebastia, near Nablus, West Bank (the city); central hill country (the region)
key: King Omri bought the hill of Samaria and built his capital there (1 Kings 16).
During a severe siege, four lepers found the Syrian camp deserted (2 Kings 7).
Samaria fell to Assyria, and Israel was carried into exile (2 Kings 17).
Jesus spoke with a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well (John 4).
Philip preached Christ in Samaria, and many believed and were baptized (Acts 8).

name: Pirathon
what: A town in the hill country of Ephraim, home of the judge Abdon and David's warrior Benaiah.
today: Likely Far'ata, southwest of Nablus, West Bank.
key: Abdon the Pirathonite judges Israel and is buried at Pirathon (Judges 12).
Benaiah of Pirathon is among David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23).
Benaiah of Pirathon appears in the Chronicler's list of mighty men (1 Chronicles 11).
Benaiah of Pirathon commands David's division for the eleventh month (1 Chronicles 27).

name: Jordan
what: The river flowing from the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea, the eastern boundary of Canaan.
today: Jordan River, between Israel, the West Bank, and Jordan
key: Jacob crossed the Jordan with only his staff on his way to Haran (Genesis 32).
The waters stopped when the priests' feet touched them, and Israel crossed on dry ground (Joshua 3).
Elijah struck the water with his cloak, and he and Elisha crossed over (2 Kings 2).
Naaman washed seven times in the Jordan and was healed of leprosy (2 Kings 5).
Jesus was baptized by John in the Jordan (Matthew 3).

name: Cherith
what: A brook east of the Jordan where God fed Elijah through ravens during the drought.
today: Exact site unknown; a wadi east of the Jordan, possibly Wadi el-Yabis, Jordan.
key: God told Elijah to hide by the brook Cherith, east of the Jordan (1 Kings 17).
Ravens brought Elijah bread and meat morning and evening, and he drank from the brook (1 Kings 17).
When the brook dried up, God sent Elijah to a widow in Zarephath (1 Kings 17).

name: Jordan Valley
what: The well-watered lowland along the Jordan River near the Dead Sea, where Lot chose to settle.
today: The Jordan Valley north of the Dead Sea, between Israel, the West Bank, and Jordan.
key: Lot saw that the Jordan Valley was well watered like the garden of the Lord (Genesis 13).
Lot chose the Jordan Valley and moved his tents as far as Sodom (Genesis 13).

name: Erech
what: An ancient city in the land of Shinar, among the first cities of Nimrod's kingdom.
today: Warka (ancient Uruk) in southern Iraq.
key: Nimrod's kingdom began with Babel, Erech, and Accad in the land of Shinar (Genesis 10).
Men of Erech were among the peoples settled in Samaria who wrote against Jerusalem's rebuilding (Ezra 4).

name: Thebez
what: A town near Shechem where Abimelech was mortally wounded by a millstone a woman dropped.
today: Likely Tubas, northeast of Nablus, West Bank.
key: Abimelech captured Thebez, but its people shut themselves inside a strong tower (Judges 9).
A woman dropped a millstone on Abimelech's head, and his armor-bearer killed him (Judges 9).
Joab expected David to recall Abimelech's death at Thebez when hearing of Uriah's death (2 Samuel 11).

name: Abel-meholah
what: A town in the Jordan Valley and hometown of the prophet Elisha.
today: Exact site uncertain; in the Jordan Valley south of Beth-shean.
key: The fleeing Midianites run toward the border of Abel-meholah after Gideon's attack (Judges 7).
Abel-meholah lies within the district of Solomon's officer Baana (1 Kings 4).
God tells Elijah to anoint Elisha son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah as prophet (1 Kings 19).

name: Shamir
what: A town in the hill country of Ephraim where the judge Tola lived and was buried.
today: Exact site unknown.
key: Tola son of Puah, a man of Issachar, lived at Shamir in Ephraim's hill country (Judges 10).
After judging Israel twenty-three years, Tola died and was buried at Shamir (Judges 10).

name: Jabesh-gilead
what: A town in Gilead east of the Jordan, closely tied to King Saul.
today: Possibly Tell el-Maqlub on Wadi Yabis in northern Jordan.
key: Israel struck Jabesh-gilead for not joining the assembly, and its young women were given to Benjamin (Judges 21).
Saul rescued Jabesh-gilead from Nahash the Ammonite (1 Samuel 11).
